notes.meaning: Jude introduces himself as a servant of Jesus Christ and the brother of James. He writes to Christians everywhere, describing them as people called by God, deeply loved by the Father, and guarded safely for Jesus. Rather than boasting about his family tie to Jesus, he counts it his highest honor to be His devoted servant.

Jude prays that God will richly multiply mercy, peace, and love for his readers. Mercy pardons our guilt, peace quiets our troubled hearts, and love knits believers together. He asks that these gifts overflow in their daily lives instead of coming in small amounts.

Jude originally planned to write about the salvation that all Christians share together. Urgent dangers forced him to change his plan and plead with them to contend, or wrestle hard, for the truth. God gave this message once for all through the apostles, so believers must guard it carefully and never change it.

Dangerous teachers had slipped quietly into the church without being noticed. They claimed that God's forgiveness gave them permission to live wildly immoral lives. By acting this way, they practically disowned Jesus Christ, their only true Master and Lord.

differ.view: The phrase means these corrupt men were marked out for condemnation long ago by God's eternal counsel and sovereign providence.
The text refers to ancient warnings and prophecies written down long ago, not to an eternal decree forcing anyone to destruction.

notes.meaning: Jude reminds his friends of historical facts they had already learned. The Lord brought the Israelites safely out of slavery in Egypt through great miracles. Yet when those same people refused to trust Him in the desert, He destroyed them.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Several of the oldest Greek manuscripts read 'Jesus' instead of 'the Lord,' pointing to the eternal Son at work delivering and then judging Israel in the wilderness.

notes.meaning: God also dealt strictly with the angels who rebelled against Him. They refused to stay within their assigned roles and left their glorious home in heaven. God has placed them in dark, unbreakable spiritual chains where they wait for their final judgment on the great day.

The ancient cities of Sodom and Gomorrah abandoned themselves to sexual sins and unnatural lusts. God wiped them out with fire from heaven as a lasting public warning. Their complete destruction stands as a picture of the eternal punishment that awaits unrepentant sinners.

Despite these awful lessons from history, the false teachers live in a fog of foolish daydreams. They ruin their bodies with shameful deeds, refuse to obey proper leadership, and insult glorious beings in the spiritual world. Their pride blinds them to the real danger of their actions.

Even the chief angel, Michael, showed great humility and self-control. When he argued with the devil over the body of Moses, he did not dare to trade insults or bring a slanderous charge against Satan. Instead, he left the judgment to God, simply saying, 'The Lord rebuke you!'

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early Christian writers noted that this incident was preserved in Jewish tradition and in a book called the Assumption of Moses, which Jude quoted to illustrate a true event without endorsing the whole book as Scripture.

notes.meaning: These deceitful men boldly attack and mock holy things they cannot understand. They live only by their bodily urges, just like wild animals that have no reason. Those very animal appetites end up ruining their lives and dragging them to destruction.

Jude pronounces deep sorrow and doom over these deceivers. They act like Cain by hating their brothers, rush like Balaam into error for money, and perish like Korah by rebelling against God's appointed order. Their lives follow the exact pattern of the worst sinners in Israel's history.

These men are like dangerous hidden rocks that can wreck a ship during the church's shared fellowship meals. They care only about indulging themselves, showing no reverence for God or concern for others. Jude calls them rainless clouds blown by the wind and dead, uprooted autumn trees that never bear fruit.

These noisy leaders resemble stormy sea waves that churn up dirty froth, exposing their own disgraceful deeds for everyone to see. They are like wandering stars that drift off course and can never guide a sailor safely. God has prepared a place of utter, eternal darkness for them.

Long before the great flood, Enoch announced that the Lord would come with countless thousands of His holy angels. God will arrive to carry out justice on all humanity and convict every ungodly person for their wicked actions and defiant words. That ancient warning applies directly to the false teachers of Jude's day.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Jude is quoting a passage from the ancient Jewish Book of Enoch, citing its well-known message to affirm a true prophecy without making the non-biblical book part of the Bible.

notes.meaning: These troublemakers are never happy, constantly complaining about their lot in life while chasing their own selfish desires. They use loud, arrogant talk to make themselves look important. Yet they will shamelessly flatter rich and powerful people whenever it brings them personal gain.

Jude urges his readers to recall what the apostles of Jesus Christ had taught them. The apostles warned that in the last days, mockers would appear inside the church who sneer at the truth and follow their own corrupt cravings. Remembering these warnings keeps believers from being shocked or led astray.

These corrupt teachers break up the church by creating selfish cliques and divisions. Even though they pretend to have special spiritual insight, they are purely worldly people. They do not have the Holy Spirit living inside them at all.

True Christians must take a completely different path by building their lives on the foundation of the holy gospel. Prayer is the great tool that helps their faith grow. Believers must pray with the guidance, power, and help of the Holy Spirit.

Believers are told to stay close to God by living in His love and obeying His truth. At the same time, they look forward with steady hope to the return of Jesus Christ. That eternal life is not something we earn, but a gift that comes purely through His mercy.

differ.view: Believers are held secure forever by God, so keeping oneself means enjoying fellowship with God, not working to prevent the loss of salvation.
Believers must actively watch and persevere in obedience, because presuming on past mercy without remaining faithful puts a soul in real danger.

notes.meaning: Jude explains how to help people who have been misled. Church members should treat wavering doubters with tender mercy and patient instruction. Others who are in immediate danger of ruin must be snatched away quickly like items pulled from a fire, while helpers stay on guard so they are not tainted by the sin.

The letter ends with a joyous song of praise to the only wise God, who rescues us through Jesus Christ our Lord. He alone has the mighty power to protect His people from stumbling into ruin. One day He will welcome them into His glorious presence, completely blameless and filled with boundless joy.
